newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy calls emergency over Albanian influx.
newsitem.headline: Italy calls emergency over Albanian influx.

text.p: Italy announced emergency measures on Wednesday to cope with a flood of Albanian refugees and military sources said the country had begun forcibly repatriating presumed "undesirables".

The special measures were adopted at a two-hour cabinet meeting on how to confront the crisis as a motley armada of decrepit boats continued to limp into southeastern ports carrying Albanians escaping the turmoil in their Balkan homeland.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini cautioned that the exodus, which has brought more than 10,000 Albanians across the Adriatic since March 13, posed a threat to all of Europe.

He said a European Union plan to help Albania end armed anarchy sparked by the failure of shady savings schemes and to provide emergency relief was intended to favour a peaceful, political end to the chaos in the continent's poorest country.
"It is also designed to ease the flow of refugees, whose consequences concern not only Italy but all of Europe," a government statement quoted Dini as telling the cabinet.
The statement said ministers had declared a "state of emergency" throughout Italy until June 30.
The measure will ease access to the emergency funds needed to care for the refugees and give wider decision-making powers to local authorities, political sources said.

The meeting confirmed that Italy would grant temporary shelter to genuine refugees but the statement said a cabinet decree law on the influx also contained provisions to repatriate "persons deemed to be a danger to public security".

Military sources said a repatriation of "undesirables" had begun on Wednesday morning, using three giant Chinook helicopters with paratroops on board to ferry some 290 Albanians to Tirana from the southeast port of Brindisi.
Italy faced a severe crisis in 1991 when some 40,000 Albanians commandeered rusting freighters and poured across the Adriatic after the collapse of 45 years of Stalinist rule.
It has since grappled with continuing problems of illegal Albanian immigration and drugs and arms-smuggling.
Several escaped prisoners from jails stormed in Albania's unrest and suspected mobsters have used the latest exodus to slip into Italy, according to ministers.

Ministers said they had strong evidence that racketeers in the Albanian port of Durres had taken control of the exodus. Albanians say they have been charged up to $600 each for a place on a boat to a new life abroad.

The scale of the exodus has taken Italy by surprise. Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano told parliament that Italy had planned shelter for 3,500 refugees but nearly three times that number had poured in.
"The wave and rhythm of arrivals from Albania...has exceeded every possible forecast," he said on Tuesday, adding that Italy intended to send refugees home as soon as the situation allowed.
"We will offer shelter for as long as civil life in Albania remains deeply disturbed and no longer," Napolitano said.
Refugees continued to reach shore on Wednesday, including some 200 who had to be rescued by Italian coastguard vessels from a stricken Albanian tug 20 miles off the Albanian coast.
Coastguard sources said 60 to 70 percent of the Albanian naval and merchant fleet had already been used in the exodus. Those boats have been impounded on arrival in Italy.
"Whether the exodus continues will depend on how seaworthy the vessels left in Albania are," one coastguard source said.

He cautioned, however, that cases had already emerged of unfit boats being towed out of Albanian waters and left to drift in the hope that their passengers would be rescued by Italian or U.S. Navy ships in the Adriatic.
